A qualification record is only as useful as what it retains. At minimum, a resistance-welding qualification record should retain each of the following, because each answers a specific question an auditor, customer or root-cause investigator will eventually ask:

- Test-piece identification — so a specific physical sample can be traced back to the record that describes it.

- Material and thickness records — confirming exactly what was tested, not just what was intended.

- The exact equipment configuration used — controller, transformer, gun and secondary-circuit configuration as actually run.

- Welding parameters actually run (not just targeted) — the measured, executed values, which can differ from the programmed nominal values.

- Electrode information — type, material/class and geometry as used in the qualification trials.

- Test method and results — which inspection/test method was used and what it found.

- Observed failure modes — e.g. button pull-out versus interfacial failure (Chapter 10, Testing and Quality Verification).

- Measurements and the acceptance decision — the actual numbers and the pass/fail determination made against them.

- Approvals/signatures — who authorized the qualification and when.

6. Linear, Orbital and Radial Friction Welding

The rotary variants require at least one component to be axisymmetric about the joint. Three variants remove that constraint:

Linear friction welding (424). One component oscillates linearly against the other at high frequency and small amplitude under axial pressure. Because no rotation is involved, non-axisymmetric components can be joined — the process's defining advantage. Its principal industrial application is aerospace: joining blades to discs to form integrally bladed rotors, where the joint geometry is a blade root, not a cylinder.

Orbital friction welding (426). Relative motion follows a small circular orbit rather than rotation about the joint axis, so every point on the interface traces the same small circle. Also suits non-axisymmetric parts, and gives more uniform interface velocity than rotary welding, where velocity varies from zero at the centre to maximum at the periphery.

Radial friction welding (425). A ring is rotated and compressed radially onto the outside of two abutting components, welding them together. Used for pipe joining, where the internal bore must remain unobstructed.

1. Joint Type and Weld Type Are Two Different Decisions

These two terms are used interchangeably in conversation and they mean different things. The joint type is the geometric arrangement of the parts — how the two pieces of metal are placed relative to each other. The weld type is what is deposited into that arrangement.

The distinction is practical rather than pedantic: a T-joint can be made with a fillet weld, with a partial-penetration groove weld, with a full-penetration groove weld, or with a combination of groove and fillet. Those four choices have different strengths, different costs, different inspection requirements and different distortion behaviour. Specifying "a T-joint" says nothing about which. Every drawing dispute over welding traces back to one party naming the joint and the other assuming the weld.

11. Materials and Dissimilar Combinations

Similar-metal joints: carbon and alloy steels, stainless steels, tool steels, aluminium alloys, copper alloys, nickel alloys and titanium are all routinely friction welded. Hardenable steels require attention to the post-weld cooling and frequently a post-weld heat treatment (Section 14).

Dissimilar joints are a principal reason to choose the process. Because interface temperature is below melting, time at temperature is very short, and reacted material is expelled into the flash, intermetallic formation is limited in a way fusion welding cannot achieve (Chapter 27, Section 2).

Combinations commonly made by friction welding that are difficult or impossible by fusion welding:

• Aluminium to steel — with careful control of upset and time to keep the intermetallic layer thin.

• Copper to aluminium and copper to steel.

• Titanium to steel — feasible in some configurations where fusion welding is not.

• Tool steel to structural steel — the classic application for cutting tool shanks, where an expensive tool material is joined to a cheap shank.

• Stainless to carbon steel.

5. The Coil and the Field Shaper

The coil must carry an extremely large current for a few microseconds while withstanding the reaction force. Coils are made of high-strength, high-conductivity material and are frequently reinforced. Their geometry — usually a single or few turns around the workpiece — determines the field distribution and therefore where the force is applied.

The field shaper is a separate conductive insert placed between the coil and the workpiece. It carries induced current from the coil's field and re-concentrates that field into a smaller, precisely defined region at its inner surface.

Why it matters practically:

• It concentrates the force where the joint is, improving efficiency.

• It defines the weld zone geometry precisely.

• It protects the coil by taking the mechanical and electrical duty at the working surface — the field shaper is a cheaper, replaceable item, and coil life improves substantially with one.

• It allows one coil to serve several part sizes by changing only the field shaper.

Field shapers are consumables and their wear changes the process, so their condition and replacement interval belong in the process control.

The cooling path in a typical installation runs from a chiller or plant-water source, through a supply/return manifold, through hoses and fittings, through filters/strainers, through flow monitoring and temperature monitoring, through heat exchangers, and finally into the actual cooling passages inside the gun, transformer and electrodes. 4. Plasma Cutting

The mechanism: an arc is struck between an electrode and the workpiece and constricted through a nozzle orifice, exactly as in plasma arc welding (Chapter 42, Section 2) but at higher gas flow and with the deliberate objective of blowing the molten metal out of the kerf rather than containing it. The plasma jet melts the metal and its kinetic energy ejects it.

Because it melts rather than oxidizes, it cuts any electrically conductive metal — stainless, aluminium, copper, nickel alloys and carbon steel alike. That is its decisive advantage over oxy-fuel.

Variants:

• Conventional plasma — air or oxygen plasma, general purpose.

• High-definition / precision plasma — additional constriction and gas management producing a narrower, squarer, higher-quality cut, closing much of the gap to laser cutting.

• Underwater plasma — cutting with the plate submerged, which dramatically reduces noise, fume and radiation, and reduces distortion. A genuine and under-used option for production cutting.

4. Advancing and Retreating Sides

The weld is not symmetric, and this asymmetry is fundamental rather than incidental.

On one side of the joint, the tool's rotational velocity is in the same direction as the traverse — the advancing side. On the other, it opposes the traverse — the retreating side.

Consequences:

• Material flow is asymmetric. Material is swept from the advancing side around the pin and deposited on the retreating side.

• The advancing side has a sharp, well-defined boundary between the stirred zone and the parent material; the retreating side has a diffuse, gradual boundary.

• Defects concentrate on the advancing side, particularly voids and tunnel defects, because that is where flow is most demanding.

• In dissimilar joints, which material is placed on the advancing side changes the result, and this is a genuine process variable that must be fixed in the procedure.

An engineer looking at a friction stir weld section can identify the advancing side by the sharp boundary, and knowing which side it was is often the first step in diagnosing a defect.

6. Solidification Structure and Where It Goes Wrong

Weld metal solidifies epitaxially: the first solid forms on the existing grains at the fusion boundary and continues their crystallographic orientation. There is no nucleation barrier to overcome, so the weld metal grain structure is seeded directly by the parent grain structure at the fusion line.

Growth then proceeds competitively — grains oriented favourably relative to the steepest thermal gradient outgrow their neighbours — producing the coarse columnar grains that run from the fusion boundary toward the weld centreline in almost every fusion weld. The direction those columns take is set by the shape of the trailing pool boundary, which is set by travel speed. A slow weld has a roughly elliptical pool and columnar grains that curve gently to meet at the centreline; a fast weld has a teardrop-shaped pool and columnar grains that meet the centreline head-on in a straight, continuous plane.

5. Titanium: Welding Inside a Controlled Atmosphere

Titanium is not difficult to melt and not especially crack-sensitive. It is difficult because it reacts with the atmosphere at welding temperature, and the reaction products embrittle it irreversibly.

Above roughly 400 °C, titanium absorbs oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen from the air. These dissolve interstitially and raise strength while destroying ductility and toughness. There is no post-weld heat treatment that removes them — the contamination is dissolved in the metal, not a surface scale to be cleaned off. A contaminated titanium weld is scrap.

3. Range of Approval: Thickness

The test coupon thickness determines the production thickness range the welder may weld. Under ISO 9606-1 the ranges are banded by test thickness, with the general pattern that a test on material of thickness *t* qualifies from a stated minimum up to 2t [S2].

For example, a test on a 12 mm plate butt weld gives a range of approval from 3 mm to 24 mm [S2].

Two practical consequences:

Testing thicker qualifies more. A shop that tests everyone on thin material to save consumables and time will find its welders unqualified for the heavier work in the same production mix.

The lower bound is real. A qualification on heavy plate does not automatically extend down to sheet thicknesses, because thin material is a genuinely different manipulation problem — the risk changes from lack of fusion to burn-through.

Oxy-fuel cutting is chemically distinct from the other two, and the distinction determines everything about where it can be used.

The mechanism:

1. A preheat flame (Chapter 63) heats a spot on the steel to its ignition temperature — the temperature at which it will burn in oxygen, which is below its melting point.

2. A jet of pure oxygen is directed at that spot through a central orifice in the nozzle.

3. The steel burns in the oxygen stream — an exothermic oxidation reaction producing iron oxide and a great deal of heat.

4. The oxygen jet's kinetic energy blows the molten oxide out of the kerf.

QUESTION: What is the mechanism of oxy-fuel cutting?

text:
Chemical oxidation of the metal in a jet of pure oxygen — carbon and low-alloy steels only.

-Shielded FCAW and Why It Works Without Gas

Self-shielded wire generates its entire protective atmosphere from the core, and the chemistry is genuinely different rather than merely more concentrated.

The mechanism. Beyond gas-forming and slag-forming constituents, the core carries strong denitriders and deoxidizers — aluminium in particular — in quantities calculated to scavenge the nitrogen and oxygen that inevitably reach the pool from the surrounding air. The process does not exclude the atmosphere the way a gas shield does; it tolerates partial atmospheric contact and neutralizes the consequences chemically.

Three things follow directly, and all three are frequently violated in practice:

1. Self-shielded wire must never be run under a shielding gas. Doing so removes the oxygen and nitrogen the scavenging chemistry was designed to consume, leaving an over-deoxidized deposit with degraded toughness. The result looks fine and tests badly.

2. Electrode extension (stick-out) is a controlled variable, not a preference. The scavenging reactions depend on the resistive preheating of the wire extension, and self-shielded wires are formulated for a specific, generally long, stick-out range. Running short defeats the chemistry.

Step 1 — Classify by timing. The joint passed fabrication testing and failed after two years of thermal cycling at elevated temperature. This is a service degradation mechanism, not a fabrication defect that was missed. Framing the investigation as "the radiography must have been inadequate" would send it in the wrong direction from the start.

text:
The joint passed radiography and hydrostatic testing at fabrication, so the leak is a service degradation mechanism — a crack running close to the fusion boundary on the carbon steel side.

Noise. Air carbon arc gouging and plasma cutting are genuinely high-noise operations requiring hearing protection; most arc welding is not, but the associated grinding and chipping is.

Heat stress. Radiant heat from the arc and the workpiece, plus heavy protective clothing, plus confined or elevated positions. Manageable with work-rest cycles, hydration and cooling, and worth explicit planning in hot climates and in vessel interiors, where heat exhaustion also degrades judgement about every other hazard on this list.

Ergonomics. Sustained awkward postures, overhead work, vibration from grinders and manual handling of cylinders and assemblies. Musculoskeletal disorders are among the most common causes of long-term absence in fabrication.

Electromagnetic fields. Welding currents generate strong fields close to cables and the workpiece. The established precautions are to keep cables together and close to the body's side rather than draped around the torso, avoid coiling cable around the body, and keep the welder's body away from the loop formed by the electrode and return cables. People with implanted medical devices such as pacemakers must obtain specific medical advice before working near welding equipment.

11. Fault Family 8 — Dimensional and Distortion Problems

Symptom: the assembly is out of tolerance, or moves during or after welding.

Causes: excessive heat input; oversized welds; unbalanced welding sequence; welds placed away from the neutral axis; inadequate or excessive restraint; machining after welding releasing residual stress.

Actions: reduce weld size to the drawing requirement; balance the sequence about the neutral axis; use back-step or skip sequences; pre-set or pre-bend; improve fixturing — while recognizing that restraint converts distortion into residual stress and increases cracking risk on sensitive material (Chapter 22, Section 11).

Step 2 — On cracking, work the contamination list before anything else. Nickel alloys crack from sulphur, phosphorus, lead and zinc at low concentrations. The questions are concrete and answerable on the shop floor: what marking materials were used on the nozzle; was the surface degreased immediately before welding or earlier; were fixtures or backing bars previously used on galvanized or leaded work; was any galvanized cutting done nearby; were clean gloves used. In a shop with previous success, the useful question is what changed — a new marker, a different bench, a new operator's habits.

Step 3 — Check dilution as the second cracking candidate. An overlay's first layer is heavily diluted by the carbon steel substrate, and excessive iron pickup shifts the deposit composition away from the region the filler was designed for. If parameters were run hotter than qualified — higher current, slower travel, more weave — dilution rises. Measuring the deposit chemistry of the first layer settles this directly, and it is the standard acceptance check for corrosion-resistant overlay work in any case.

Sulphur, phosphorus, lead and zinc at low concentrations.

Step 2 — Establish the weldability window in both directions, which is the core of the qualification. Weld a matrix of samples across a range of charge energies and standoff gaps, and section each. The results define: the lower boundary, below which no bond forms (crimp only); the upper boundary, above which the interface melts and intermetallics appear; and the region between, where a regular wavy interface forms.

Step 3 — Section and read the interfaces properly. For each sample, record whether waves are present and regular, whether melted pockets appear at wave vortices, and — critically for this couple — whether an intermetallic layer is present and how thick it is. This is the measurement that matters for an aluminium-steel joint, and it is why metallography rather than mechanical testing must lead the qualification.

Resistance spot welding (RSW) is a resistance-welding process that produces a weld at the faying (contacting) surfaces between overlapping parts, using heat obtained from the resistance to the flow of welding current through the parts, combined with the application of mechanical force through the electrodes [S9]. It belongs to the pressure-welding family: unlike arc or laser welding, no filler metal is added and no arc is struck. The joint forms entirely from localized resistive heating under clamping force, which is why the process is sometimes described to newcomers as "welding by squeezing and cooking," a simplification that is directionally correct even though it skips the electrical detail that actually governs weld quality.
